Chapter 3. Rethinking What It Means to Be “Civilized”
When you hear the word “civilization,” what pops into your mind? Maybe it’s grand cities, impressive achievements, or that constant sense of moving forward. There’s no denying—civilization carries a certain weight. But if you dig a little deeper, you’ll see that being “civilized” is actually a lot more complicated, and sometimes, more limiting, than it seems at first glance.
Picture this. A group of friends gathered around a kitchen table, chatting late into the night. The talk drifts from work, to politics, to what the future might hold. Someone sighs and wonders why life feels so rushed, so scattered. Another friend mentions that, for most of human history, people lived in tight-knit groups. Everyone had a say, and each person mattered. Suddenly, the room goes quiet as everyone takes in just how much we might’ve lost in our sprint toward modern life.
The thing is, civilization—as we know it—runs on hierarchy and control. There are leaders and there are followers, rules and consequences, winners and losers. The whole system seems designed to reward those who fit the mold, and push aside anyone who doesn’t. Sure, it promises us order and security, but too often, what we actually get is stress and a sense of being cut off from others.
Now, a lot of folks believe that without civilization, all you’d have left is chaos—every person out for themselves, with no rules at all. But that’s not really how it works. For thousands of years, people lived in ways that were neither wild nor rigid. They organized themselves into tribes—not “primitive,” but groups built on mutual support and a sense of shared purpose.
In these tribal setups, power wasn’t hoarded at the top. Instead, it was spread out. Decisions happened through conversation and agreement, not by someone barking orders. People helped each other—not because they had to, but because their lives depended on it. There weren’t prisons or police because everyone was invested in the group’s well-being.
For most people today, it’s tough to even imagine living like that. Giving up the comforts of civilization? That sounds impossible. But here’s the thing: tribal living isn’t about ditching technology or heading back to the Stone Age. It’s about rethinking how we connect with each other—moving from competition to real collaboration, from strict hierarchies to genuine partnership.
And it’s already happening in small ways. There are worker-owned businesses, intentional communities, and cooperative housing popping up all over. These aren’t perfect, but they prove something important: it’s possible to build a life around shared values, without someone always calling the shots from above.
The biggest hurdle isn’t technology—it’s the way we’ve been taught to think. Most of us grew up believing we’re just individuals, fighting over limited resources. The idea of sharing power and responsibility can feel pretty strange. But once people actually try it, even in little ways, something changes. Life starts to feel less scary, and suddenly, a different kind of future doesn’t seem so far-fetched.
So, rethinking what it means to be “civilized” isn’t about tossing out everything that’s come before. It’s about realizing that the world we know is just one option among many. If we look to the past—not to copy it, but to find inspiration—we can start to imagine new ways of living. Ways that are more sustainable, more just, and a whole lot more satisfying.
